newsitem.title: USA: U.S. spinoffs seen pricier, tougher in future.
newsitem.headline: U.S. spinoffs seen pricier, tougher in future.

text.p: U.S. companies seeking to spin off units may raise the selling price for their properties or restructure transactions if federal legislators kill a popular provision that permits tax-free deals.
Legislation to eliminate the so-called "Morris Trust" provision also would force sellers to find creative ways to unload units or find more value in non-core subsidiaries, Wall Street experts said.
"Sellers will be raising their asking prices or they may decide not to sell at all," said Philip Keevil, managing director at Salomon Brothers.
Investment bankers and tax experts said the potential death of Morris Trust is likely to affect some pending transactions, but will likely have little overall impact on deal activity.

Although Morris Trust spin-offs have become increasingly popular in the past few years as corporate America has embraced slim-downed and narrowly-focused strategies, they still comprise just a fraction of overall corporate transactions.

"It could put a damper on activity, but at the same time I think managements are going to pursue those strategic transactions that are going to have the most long-term benefit to the shareholders in today's environment," said Ned Weihman of Wasserstein Perella & Co.
"Companies are going to sell their businesses and accept the tax consequences, but it's going to cost the acquirer more," said Barbara Goodstein, a spinoff expert at Rothschild Inc.

Although the legislation was formally introduced in Congress last week, the Morris Trust provision has been under attack for a while and was targeted for elimination in President Clinton's budget introduced in February.
Under a Morris Trust transaction, the seller spins off unwanted units to stockholders as a separate company and then merges the rest of the firm with a buyer in a tax-free deal.
"Morris-Trust is an efficient way to distribute value to your shareholders without taking a bite out for the tax man," said Weihman.
The impact of the death of Morris Trust is already having implications. If enacted, the legislation would be effective as of April 16 and therefore would affect deals announced last week.

Airtouch Communications Inc. and U S West Media Group said last week their proposed transaction, in which US West will merge its domestic wireless cable with Airtouch in a $5 billion stock deal, could be blocked by elimination of Morris Trust and would force them to continue their existing joint venture agreement.
Sources also have said that talks between America Online Inc. and CompuServe Corp. are also being hampered in part by the legislation.
"That transaction was always a tough one and this has to make it tougher," said one investment banker.
Several other bankers also said they were involved in potential transactions that would likely be restructured.

"To me, it's not cataclysmic. As long as the market is saying it appreciates a simple business that's not in multiple lines of commerce, spinoffs will continue to happen," said one banker who did not want to be identified.

So far this year, there have been a handful of large transactions structured under the Morris Trust provision, including Raytheon Co. 's announced $9.5 billion acquisition of General Motors' Hughes Electronics Corp.

"In terms of our merger, it was a very important consideration," said Keith Booke, spokesman for Valero Energy Corp., which in January announced plans to sell its natural gas business to PG&E Corp. Under that deal, Valero's refining subsidiary will be spun off prior to the merger.
